Upstar is now RatingIQ.

New name. New logo. New slogan: "From reviews to revenue."

Same team. Same stubbornly specific belief: a hotel chain's Booking.com score is a revenue number, not a PR metric.

We built the product we always wanted to build. Not another review management tool. Not a dashboard. An operational push system that maps what's hurting your score, prioritizes the fixes, and gets the right information to the right people. No waiting for anyone to log in.

The new website is live: rating-iq.com

If you're a hotel chain CEO and your rating isn't where it should be. That's exactly the conversation we want.

I once sat across from a hotel chain CEO who told me his rating wasn't a priority.

His RevPAR was down 11% that quarter.

He just hadn't connected the two yet.

A 0.2 drop on Booking.com. Barely noticeable on paper. But it quietly erases $200K+ in annual revenue for a mid-size chain.

Here's the math nobody puts on a slide:
→ Lower score = lower search rank
→ Lower rank = fewer clicks
→ Fewer clicks = lower conversion
→ Lower conversion = lower RevPAR

Everyone says "our rating dipped a bit."

That dip has a dollar amount. Most chains never find it.

We built RatingIQ to find it.

A 0.2 drop has a dollar amount. Most chains never find it.

We built RatingIQ to find it.

Something we've been building for a while is finally live.

rating-iq.com

We rebuilt everything - the product story, the way we explain what we do, and why it matters if you're running a hotel chain with a rating problem.

Here's what the site shows:

Exactly which factors are moving your rating - across every property, not just the loudest one.

Your full chain picture, broken down by platform, by segment, month by month. No more guessing where you actually stand.

Every guest review answered automatically, in the right language - so your GMs stay focused on running the hotel.

We built a rating-performance system. Not review management. Not another dashboard to log into.

Go see what that looks like.

rating-iq.com

Omri puts the math behind something I explain in every demo.

0.2 on Booking.com isn't a small dip. It's a number on the P&L.

This post is the short version of every conversation we have.

The most common thing I hear after a demo:

"Wait. This doesn't require a renovation?"

No. It doesn't.

Most hotels losing ground on their Booking.com score aren't losing it because the building is bad. They're losing it because:

Breakfast runs 20 minutes late on weekends.
Check-in at 3 PM becomes a quiet disaster.
Room 214 has a shower that's been "almost fixed" since February.

These are operational problems. They have operational fixes. No CapEx required.

The trick is knowing which ones are actually moving the score. And getting that information to the person who can act on it.

That's the whole product.

RatingIQ is not a review management tool.

Not a reputation dashboard. Not a "feedback analytics platform."

(We've seen enough of those.)

It's an operational push system for hotel chains:
→ Maps what's actually hurting the score
→ Prioritizes the fixes
→ Pushes the right actions to the right people. No login required.

Because nobody logs in.

rating-iq.com

Every hotel bought a review management tool.

A genuinely surprising number of them open it maybe twice a month.

I'm not judging. I get it. The GM is running a hotel. 47 things on fire at any given moment. Opening a dashboard to "explore patterns" is not on that list.

So the data sits. Reviews pile up. The same complaints come in every weekend. Nothing changes.

The fix isn't a better dashboard. It's a push.

New complaint cluster? Tell the GM. Don't wait for them to find it.
Same issue across 3 properties? Tell the CEO.
Score trending down? Alert someone before it shows up on the display.

That's how review data actually gets used.
You make it come to people. Not the other way around.

Hotel chains have three kinds of rating problems.

The first is visible. A score that's been sitting at 8.1 for 18 months while the city average climbs.

The second is quiet. A trailing 90-day average that's lower than the displayed score. A drop signal most chains never see coming.

The third is operational. Recurring complaints that never get mapped to a fix because nobody owns the data-to-action step.

All three are solvable. None of them require guesswork.

That's what RatingIQ is for.

From reviews to revenue.

That's the only journey that matters.

Not "manage your reputation." Not "monitor your feedback."

Move the number that moves your P&L.

rating-iq.com

The guest who gives you a 7 is more useful than the one who gives you a 10.

Hotels have this backwards.

A 10 tells you they loved it. Nothing to learn, nothing to fix.
A 3 tells you they're furious. You're in damage control. That relationship is probably over.

A 7? That guest almost had a great stay.

They noticed something specific. They cared enough to write it down. And they're not angry enough to walk away permanently.

That is a blueprint.

Hotels spend most of their energy on the 3s.
They celebrate the 10s.
They scroll past the 7s.

The 7 is telling you exactly what to fix to turn a one-time visitor into a repeat guest.

Most of the time, the fix doesn't cost anything.

The 7 is a blueprint. Most hotels scroll past it.

We built a system to make sure you don't.

rating-iq.com

The 7 is the one worth reading.

Omri explains why most hotels are focused on the wrong end of the scale. I've been saying this for months and never found a way to put it this clearly.

True story.

A chain CEO told me their rating had been stuck at 8.3 for two years.

I pulled their review data before the call.

Top complaint cluster across 4 properties: WiFi in meeting rooms.

Same issue. 11 months in a row. 47 reviews. Never once escalated to someone with authority to fix it.

Two weeks after the call, they sorted the infrastructure.

Score: 8.6 within 60 days.

No renovation. No new staff. No rebranding.

Just: someone finally connected the complaint to the person who could act on it.

That's RatingIQ.

Score up 0.3 in 60 days. No renovation. One connected complaint.

This is exactly what RatingIQ is built for.

The average hotel chain has:

→ 4 recurring complaint clusters unresolved for 90+ days
→ 1 property dragging down the portfolio average by 0.4 points
→ A Booking.com score that hasn't moved in over a year

We didn't make these numbers up. We see them every time we look at a new portfolio.

The good news: all three are fixable without touching the building.

rating-iq.com

The WiFi story. Every time I share this, someone says "we have the exact same problem."

That's the point. These aren't unusual problems. They're just unconnected ones.

The question hotel chains ask: "How do we manage our reviews?"

The question they should be asking: "What's the fastest path to a higher score?"

Those sound similar. They're completely different.

"Manage reviews" = respond faster, template better, apologize more professionally.

"Faster path to a higher score" = find what's actually hurting the rating, fix it operationally, move the number.

One of these is a PR exercise.
One shows up on the P&L.

You already know which one matters.

Mother's Day weekend is the most reviewed weekend in hospitality.

Full houses. High expectations. Staff running at capacity.

The complaints that land Monday morning after a holiday weekend are some of the most consistent, predictable patterns we see.

Same issues across chains, year after year:
Breakfast too slow. Room not ready. Spa overbooked with no waitlist system.

None of these are surprises. All of them were predictable.

Happy Mother's Day to everyone running a hotel this weekend. You've earned it.

(And if the reviews land hard on Monday, you know where to find us.)

Not all complaints are equal.

A one-off guest complaint about a specific staff member? Probably not moving your score.

A recurring cluster about check-in wait times across 3 properties for 6 weeks? That's your score.

RatingIQ shows you the difference. And pushes the fix to the people who can act on it.

Because knowing isn't enough. Someone has to do something about it.

rating-iq.com

True story.

Hotel chain. 6 properties. Booking.com scores from 7.9 to 8.7.

The CEO assumed the 7.9 property needed a renovation.

We pulled the data before he signed anything.

Top complaint cluster at the 7.9 property: a single check-in desk handling peak arrival times solo.

That's it. One operational gap. No structural issue. No design problem.

They added a second desk for peak hours.

Score: 8.4 within 90 days.

The CEO's words at our next call: "I was about to spend $400K on the wrong thing."

The most expensive mistake in this industry is solving the visible problem instead of the actual one.

The most expensive mistake in hospitality: solving the visible problem instead of the actual one.

Our founder. Our mission.

The $400K story is real. I was in that call.

The CEO was ready to sign a renovation. The data said something completely different.

This is why we pull the data before you make a decision.

Hotels that address their top 3 complaint clusters within 30 days:

→ See an average rating improvement of 0.3-0.5 points within 90 days
→ Without capital expenditure
→ Through operational prioritization alone

These aren't projections from a marketing deck.
These are outcomes from chains using RatingIQ.

The math is straightforward once you know where to look.

Hotel ratings on Booking.com are not a popularity contest.

They're a feedback loop with financial consequences.

A 0.1 point improvement in your score can shift your search rank enough to meaningfully move occupancy.

Which means the conversation isn't: "How do we get more positive reviews?"

It's: "What's actually driving our negative reviews. How fast can we fix it?"

Different question. Different answer. Different result.

The second one leads to RatingIQ.

One of the highest-demand weekends in US hospitality.

Also: one of the highest-complaint weekends.

The gap between a sold-out property and a well-reviewed sold-out property isn't square footage or thread count.

It's operational execution under pressure.

The chains that come out of this weekend with better reviews than they went in. They had the fixes mapped before Friday.

Good luck to everyone running a full house this weekend. You've earned the demand.

Your rating isn't a reputation score. It's a revenue dial.

RatingIQ shows you exactly which direction it's moving. And why.

Most people assume unhappy guests are just looking to vent. Some are. But a lot of them are looking to be heard.

When you respond. Publicly, consistently, in the right language. You change the signal you send to every guest who comes after.
